name: Hair micropigmentation

lead: Scalp micropigmentation (SMP) tattoos tiny dots onto the scalp so it looks like closely shaved hair. People use it to look like they have a buzz cut on a bald scalp, to make a thin crown look denser, or to camouflage hair-transplant and other scars.

Pigment is placed in the superficial skin and matched to the client's existing hair colour, imitating the shadow of cropped hair. The result is visible right away and is described mainly in news and magazine coverage rather than peer-reviewed studies.

paras: It typically takes about three to four sessions of around two hours each. The look is long lasting, and touch-ups are used over time. It is usually worn with a closely cropped or shaved head.
Allergic reaction to the ink is a stated concern, and a poorly placed hairline can look unnatural. Removal requires laser. No peer-reviewed studies were identified.

angle.text: Men with hair loss get scalp micropigmentation to create the look of a buzz cut, add apparent density to a thin crown, or hide transplant scars. The pigment is visible immediately, and hairline placement determines how natural it looks.

lead: Hair micropigmentation, usually called scalp micropigmentation (SMP) or a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo applied to the scalp. It is used to create the look of a closely shaved head on a bald scalp, to add apparent density to a thinning crown, or to conceal hair-transplant scars and other scars on the head [1].

Wikipedia describes the procedure as typically taking three to four sessions of about two hours each, with pigment matched to the colour of the client's existing hair. It is described as long lasting but removable by laser [1]. The article cites news and magazine coverage rather than peer-reviewed studies [1].

paras: The technique deposits pigment in the superficial skin to imitate hair follicles. Practitioners may perform a small patch test first for ink allergy, and the hairline is described as the most important part of the work, with a poorly executed hairline looking unnatural [1]. The hairline can reportedly be adjusted or touched up over time [1].
Coverage of celebrity scalp tattoos appeared in The Hollywood Reporter in 2013, and ABC News and Men's Health ran pros-and-cons pieces in 2012 and 2013 respectively [1].

Wikipedia states allergic reactions are a concern that patch testing aims to address, and that no scientific data on long-term side effects have been reported over the past decade when reputable ink is used, a statement that carries a citation-needed tag on that page [1].
